prompt.context: Pharma Co. has developed a new AML drug X (a type of cancer). Preliminary Phase I trials indicate tremendous potential, but the costs to get the drug FDA approved and to market are extremely high. A private equity firm has approached Pharma Co. offering to pay $150M for 50% of all future drug X profits.
prompt.question: Pharma Co. wants you to tell it what to do: should it accept the private equity firm's offer of $150M for 50% of all future drug X profits, or proceed independently?

clarifying_info.a: The only known objective is to determine how Pharma Co. should proceed.

clarifying_info.q: Does Pharma Co. have experience taking a drug to market?
clarifying_info.a: No, Pharma Co. has no experience taking a drug to market.

clarifying_info.q: How expensive is drug X for patients?
clarifying_info.a: Cancer drugs tend to be extremely expensive — $100k+ for the patient.
Only U.S. insurance will reimburse the cost of drug X, so Pharma Co. only wants to consider the U.S. market.

clarifying_info.q: Does Pharma Co. have other drugs in development?
clarifying_info.a: Yes, Pharma Co. does have other drugs in the pipeline.

clarifying_info.q: What stage are the FDA trials?
clarifying_info.a: Drug X has not completed U.S. FDA Phase I, Phase II, or Phase III trials.
Assume a patent life of 10 years.
Side effects are consistent with similar drugs — treat as a non-factor.

exhibits.title: Market Inputs and Competitor Market Share by Year
exhibits.shows: Key market input assumptions and a table of competitor market share by year (YR1 through YR11)

exhibits.title: Phase and Production Costs
exhibits.shows: Costs broken down by FDA trial phase (Phase I, II, III) and production cost components as percentages of price

data.phase_I_cost: $160M (includes amount already invested plus projected amount to complete Phase I trials)

framework: Market opportunity: estimate total addressable market using patient population, pricing, willingness to prescribe, ramp-up, competition, and patent life
Risk adjustment: apply FDA trial success probabilities (Phase I, II, III) to both revenue and costs to get risk-adjusted figures
Cost analysis: identify and quantify non-recurring costs (R&D, trial phases) and recurring costs (manufacturing, logistics, other production)
Deal evaluation: compare risk-adjusted EBITDA to the PE firm's offer ($150M for 50% of profits); assess NPV of the 50% profit stream
Strategic factors: Pharma Co.'s lack of experience, capital needs, pipeline synergies, alternative structures (partner, license, sell), risk tolerance

questions.prompt: What information would you want to collect to determine total market opportunity, and how would you collect it?
questions.guidance: Strong answers identify multiple sources: expert interviews (doctors, insurance, pharma business, healthcare experts), government census / demographic data, medical journals for AML incidence trends, FDA records of competitive drug trials, adoption ramp data for similar drugs, patient surveys on willingness to try drug X, price benchmarks from similar drugs, competitor financial reports and pipeline data, and government contract benchmarks (e.g., Medicare)

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 1, calculate the total market opportunity for drug X over the patent life.
questions.guidance: Candidate should apply willingness-to-prescribe rate to annual patients, then apply ramp assumption (reaching 100% after Year 3), then apply Pharma Co.'s market share (100% in YR1-4, 75% in YR5-10 after 25% competitor entry), then multiply by price per patient, then sum over 10 years.

math.setup: Annual patients afflicted = 3,300; willingness-to-prescribe = 70% → 2,310 addressable patients. Market share: 100% YR1-4, 75% YR5-10. Ramp: 11% YR1, 55% YR2, 100% YR3+. Price = $125,000/patient/year.
math.answer: ~$2.07B total market opportunity over the 10-year patent life

questions.prompt: The drug has not yet completed FDA trials. Apply the phase success probabilities to calculate the risk-adjusted market opportunity. Phase I: 90%, Phase II: 30%, Phase III: 50%.
questions.guidance: Candidate should multiply the probabilities together to get total approval probability, then apply to the total market opportunity. Should recognize that each phase probability is conditional on passing the prior phase.

math.setup: Total probability = Phase I x Phase II x Phase III = 90% x 30% x 50%
math.answer: Total FDA approval probability: 13.5%; Risk-adjusted market opportunity: ~$280M

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, what costs should be considered, and calculate total risk-adjusted costs (EBITDA input).
questions.guidance: Candidate should first brainstorm cost categories (regulatory fees, promotional materials, marketing, production/manufacturing, personnel, facilities, packaging, logistics, distribution, taxes), then use Exhibit 2 to calculate risk-adjusted costs by applying the cumulative phase probabilities to each phase cost and to production costs. A strong candidate notes the distinction between non-recurring (trial phases) and recurring (production) costs.

math.setup: Risk-adjust each cost bucket by the probability of reaching that stage. Phase I cost already includes sunk + future. Production costs apply only if all phases pass (13.5% probability). Total revenue base for production = ~$2B.
steps: Phase II risk-adjusted: $125M x (90% x 30%) = $125M x 27% = ~$34M
Phase III risk-adjusted: $75M x (90% x 30% x 50%) = $75M x 13.5% = ~$10M

questions.prompt: The PE firm is offering $150M for 50% of all future drug X profits. How would you evaluate this offer using NPV? (Discount rate: 5%)
questions.guidance: Candidate should explain how to structure the NPV: discount the 50% profit stream (50% of ~$38M EBITDA = ~$19M per year equivalent) over the patent life at 5%. Should recognize the NPV will likely be negative relative to $150M. Strong candidate notes NPV of 50% profit stream is approximately -$25M (i.e., accepting $150M today is better than receiving the 50% stream). Also note that accepting the offer yields $150M + 50% of profits = ~$150M + ~$19M = ~$169M vs keeping 100% of ~$38M EBITDA.

math.setup: 50% of risk-adjusted EBITDA = 50% x $38M = ~$19M. NPV of $19M/year for ~10 years at 5% discount rate vs. receiving $150M today.
steps: Annuity PV factor at 5% for 10 years ≈ 7.72
$147M < $150M offered, so NPV of offer vs keeping 50% stream is approximately -$3M to -$25M (negative for Pharma Co. if it keeps the stream)
Accepting PE offer: $150M upfront + retain 50% of profits (~$19M/yr) = total ~$169M equivalent
Not accepting: retain 100% of $38M EBITDA but bear all risk and costs
math.answer: NPV of the 50% profit stream is approximately -$25M relative to the $150M offer; accepting the offer is financially favorable

brainstorming.prompt: What costs should Pharma Co. consider when bringing drug X to market?

categories.name: Clinical / R&D
ideas: Phase I, II, III trial costs

categories.name: Commercial / Marketing
ideas: Medical education and key opinion leader engagement

recommendation: Accept the PE firm's offer of $150M for 50% of future profits
The risk-adjusted EBITDA of ~$38M is relatively modest given a 13.5% approval probability; $150M upfront significantly de-risks Pharma Co.'s position
Total value if offer accepted: ~$150M + ~50% of realized profits, which exceeds the expected value of going alone
Pharma Co. has no prior experience taking a drug to market, making the PE partnership strategically valuable beyond just the capital
risks: Only 13.5% probability of FDA approval means most likely outcome is total loss if Pharma Co. proceeds alone
Pharma Co. lacks experience and capability to take a drug to market independently
Competitor entry starting Year 5 and patent expiry at Year 10 compress the profitable window
Risk-adjustment percentages may be conservative or optimistic — validation is needed
Accepting the offer locks in 50% profit share permanently, which is costly if the drug dramatically outperforms
next_steps: Validate FDA phase probability estimates with internal and external experts
Explore alternative deal structures: full sale of drug X rights, licensing to a pharma partner, or other equity arrangements
Reassess offer terms after Phase I completion given promising preliminary results
Evaluate whether drug X could serve as a platform/foundation for Pharma Co.'s broader pipeline
Investigate other geographies or off-label uses that could expand revenue beyond the U.S. AML market
Determine capital requirements and whether Pharma Co. could raise funds through other means
